name: Pony actor mailbox performance (100,000,000 messages) vs CAF and Charm++
baseline: CAF 0.13 (C++ Actor Framework); Charm++ 6.6.1 (C++) is in the same chart
workload: Mailbox performance benchmark: 100,000,000 messages passed between actors, plotted as speed relative to Erlang OTP 17 on 1 core against the number of physical cores (1-32), and against 32 physical cores with hyper-threading (up to 64 threads).
claimed_speedup: Read off the chart (approximate, ratios derived from page data): Pony 0.1.5 about 3.7 versus CAF 0.13 about 0.56 at 1 core (about 6.6x); about 1.67 versus 0.27 at 16 cores (about 6x); about 1.62 versus 0.19 at 32 physical cores (about 8.5x). Charm++ 6.6.1 stays below 0.1 beyond 2 cores; Erlang OTP 17 and Scala/Akka fall under 0.1 beyond about 14 cores. The hyper-threaded chart (4-64 threads) shows the same ordering, Pony about 1.5 against CAF about 0.15-0.2 at 64 threads.
tradeoffs: Pony is a separate language and runtime (actors with per-actor heaps, reference capabilities, no shared mutable state); using it from C++ means FFI or a separate process. Smaller ecosystem and a steeper learning curve than a C++ library such as CAF.
caveats: Charts only: the PDF (6 pages, gnuplot output, file creation date 2015-07-06) has no tables, so every figure here is read off the plot and is approximate. The PDF states no CPU model, compiler, optimisation flags, run count or variance, and does not link the benchmark programs; the y axis is 'speed relative to Erlang OTP 17 on 1 core', so the ratio to CAF is derived from two plotted lines. The versions are about a decade old (Pony 0.1.5, CAF 0.13, Charm++ 6.6.1, Erlang OTP 17, Scala 2.11.6 Akka); current Pony is much newer and newer CAF releases exist, so the ratio may not hold today (the qb-vs-others README, opened, names CAF 1.1.0 as current). The charts are first-party material of the Pony project, hosted in the Pony website repository, so the competitor builds are not independently tuned. The same PDF shows a loss: on 'Creating 1,048,576 actors' CAF 0.13 overtakes Pony beyond roughly 10 physical cores (about 17x versus about 9x Erlang-on-1-core at 32 cores), so this is a per-benchmark win, not a general win over CAF. www.ponylang.io (which serves this PDF) was blocked here by the egress policy, so the copy in the ponylang-website repository was used; a later Pony 0.26.0 versus CAF 0.16.3 run on 2x Xeon E5-2690 v3 listed on a doc.ic.ac.uk page was seen only as a search snippet and could not be opened, so it is not used.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'actor benchmark Savina Pony vs CAF C++ Actor Framework message passing performance results' led to the Pony benchmarks page; the PDF benchmarks_all.pdf was found in the ponylang/ponylang-website repository (docs/) via curl on raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: Lingua Franca (reactor language, C++ runtime) on the Savina actor benchmarks vs CAF
language: Lingua Franca (code generator targeting C++ and C)
baseline: CAF (C++ Actor Framework) running the same Savina benchmarks; Akka (JVM) is the second baseline
workload: Savina actor benchmark suite ported to Lingua Franca reactors (micro-benchmarks such as Ping Pong, Thread Ring, Counting, Fork Join, Big, Chameneos plus concurrency and parallelism benchmarks), execution time at a given number of worker threads.
claimed_speedup: Not on any page opened. From the abstract of the ACM TACO 2023 paper 'High-Performance Deterministic Concurrency using Lingua Franca', seen only as web search snippets (arXiv, ACM and mirrors were blocked): LF is about 1.42x faster than CAF and about 1.85-1.86x faster than Akka over the Savina suite at 20 threads, with LF behind CAF on Ping Pong and Thread Ring, ahead on Fork Join and Chameneos, and roughly on par on the parallelism benchmarks.
stars_or_usage: 329 stars (lingua-franca); benchmark repo lf-lang/benchmarks-lingua-franca has 4 stars
tradeoffs: Programs are written in the LF language and compiled by a code generator, so adopting it means a new toolchain; the generated runtime is C or C++, so this is a coordination-language and scheduler claim, not a claim that non-C/C++ machine code is faster. Deterministic semantics restrict some actor patterns (logical time, reactors).
caveats: Numbers are snippet only: the paper and its artifact data were not opened, so tier C. The public benchmark repo (lf-lang/benchmarks-lingua-franca, last commit 2026-09-20) holds the LF, Akka and CAF sources (README names CAF 0.16.5 and a patched lf-lang/savina fork) and a runner, but no result tables, no CPU model and no compiler flags; one search snippet quoted CAF 17.6, Akka 2.6.17 and an Intel i9-10900K for the paper, which conflicts with the README's CAF 0.16.5 and could not be checked. The paper's own authors built the LF side and the CAF side of the comparison. The runtime behind the win is C++, so a hand-tuned C++ actor program could probably match it; the paper also reports LF losing to CAF on Ping Pong and Thread Ring and to Akka on Counting and Big (snippet).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'actor benchmark Savina Pony vs CAF ...' and 'github Savina actor benchmark CAF Pony Akka comparison' surfaced lf-lang/benchmarks-lingua-franca; WebSearch on the paper title gave the snippet numbers.

name: Tokio async tasks vs Linux kernel threads (context-switch and creation cost, jimblandy/context-switch)
baseline: Linux kernel threads (pthreads, here created through Rust std::thread) running the same 500-stage pipe brigade; no C or C++ program is measured
workload: Context-switch benchmark: 500 tasks connected by pipes pass one byte from first to last (10,000 iterations), with a thread version and a Tokio async version; plus task creation time and resident memory per task.
claimed_speedup: README summary: context switch about 0.2 us between async tasks versus 1.7 us between kernel threads; creating a task about 0.3 us versus about 17 us for a kernel thread (about 57x, derived from page data); memory per task about 0.4 KiB versus about 20 KiB (about 9.5 KiB user plus 10 KiB kernel); 500-task brigade run: async 1.795 ms per iteration (18.19 s elapsed) versus threads 2.657 ms (26.91 s), about 1.5x; 50,000 tasks: 21 MiB versus 466 MiB resident; 250,000 async tasks run, threads stop at about 80,000 on the author's laptop.
compiler_and_flags: cargo run --release (Rust version and rustc flags not stated)
hardware: laptop with 4 cores, two-way hyper-threading, 32 GiB RAM (CPU model, kernel and distribution not stated)
tradeoffs: Tokio needs a Rust toolchain and async-colored code; the gain is in cheap tasks, not in raw throughput. The author notes the advantage vanishes when switches are driven by I/O readiness (both about 1.7 us) and that these costs are probably not the limiting factor for most applications.
caveats: Baseline is not C or C++ code: the threaded side is Rust std::thread, which on Linux is a thin wrapper over pthreads and kernel scheduling, so the numbers describe async tasks versus OS threads, and no C or C++ program was measured (the README only mentions C and C++ servers from conversations). The benchmark repo has no licence file, so the benchmark code is not copyable even though Tokio is MIT (usability mixed). Single laptop, no CPU model, no variance across machines, results quoted from one terminal session; the benchmark repo itself was last committed 2024-11-16 (tokio is active, last commit 2026-10-11). The headline advantage disappears when the threaded version is pinned to one core (taskset: 1.709 ms per iteration for threads versus 1.795 ms for async), which the author could not explain. A well-tuned C++ coroutine runtime (Boost.Asio, Boost.Fiber) is not in the comparison. Overlaps the existing Tokio 1M-tasks memory record (same project, different benchmark).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'benchmark C++20 coroutines vs Rust async vs Go goroutines vs Kotlin coroutines context switch spawn cost github results' (github.com only) surfaced jimblandy/context-switch.
why_faster: Async tasks are compiler-sized state machines (a few hundred bytes) scheduled in user space by the Tokio executor, so a task switch avoids a kernel context switch and a kernel stack; the author measures this rather than assuming it.
